what_it_does: Modern chips distribute power delivery across many small voltage regulators (called DISLDOs) scattered around the chip to keep power stable locally. The problem is that electrical noise from computation couples into the control signals that tell each regulator how much current to deliver, causing them to disagree—some push harder, some softer—leading to unstable output voltage that ripples. This design solves that by making the signal distribution itself noise-immune: it uses special analog circuit techniques so that control signals stay clean and stable even surrounded by electromagnetic noise. This lets the design deliver 2 amps of current with stable regulation, making distributed power delivery practical for advanced chips.
